q: The Greeks hid warriors inside this giant wooden structure, which the Trojans dragged into their city. Odysseus is credited with the idea. For 10 points, name this construction that ended the Trojan War, a gift that was really a trick.
Answer these questions about Greek gods and goddesses.
parts: Which winged son of Aphrodite shoots arrows that cause people to fall in love?
Which goddess is the Greek goddess of the harvest and agriculture?
Which Greek god of the forge was the husband of Aphrodite?

q: Answer these questions about the labors and adventures of Heracles.
parts: How many labors was Heracles assigned?
Heracles wore the pelt of which creature, a lion killed in his first labor?
Which many-headed water serpent, whose heads regrew when cut off, did Heracles kill with the help of Iolaus?

q: Answer these questions about the Trojan War.
parts: Which Trojan prince's abduction of Helen began the war?
Which Trojan prince was killed in single combat by Achilles?
Which king of Mycenae led the Greek forces against Troy?

q: Answer these questions about monsters of Greek myth.
parts: What creature with a lion's body and a human head killed travelers who could not answer its riddle at Thebes?
What half-woman, half-bird creatures lured sailors to their deaths with song?
What fire-breathing hybrid of a lion, a goat, and a snake was slain by Bellerophon?

q: Answer these questions about the Greek underworld.
parts: Which ferryman carried the dead across the river to the underworld?
Which river of forgetfulness did the dead drink from in the underworld?
Which river, by which the gods swore their most binding oaths, encircled the underworld?

q: Answer these questions about the Olympian goddesses.
parts: Which goddess of the hearth was the eldest sibling of Zeus?
Which winged goddess personified victory?
Which goddess of discord threw the golden apple at a wedding feast?

q: Answer these questions about Greek heroes and their quests.
parts: Which hero sailed with the Argonauts to retrieve the Golden Fleece?
Which sorceress and princess of Colchis helped the Argonauts win the Golden Fleece?
Which king of Colchis owned the Golden Fleece, guarded by a sleepless dragon?

q: Answer these questions about the creation of the Greek world.
parts: Which Titan was the father of Zeus?
What war between Zeus and the Titans was won by the Olympians?
Which Titan was condemned to hold up the sky on his shoulders?

q: This god sacrificed one of his eyes at the well of Mimir to gain wisdom and hung himself from a tree for nine nights to learn the runes. He rides an eight-legged horse and is accompanied by two ravens and two wolves. For 10 points, name this one-eyed chief of the Norse gods.

This god is the son of Odin and wields a hammer that returns to his hand after being thrown. He rides a chariot pulled by two goats and wears a belt that doubles his strength. Thunder was said to be the sound of his chariot. For 10 points, name this red-bearded Norse god of thunder.

This trickster shape-shifting caused the death of Baldr and gave birth to the horse Sleipnir after turning into a mare. He fathered the wolf Fenrir and the world serpent with a giantess. For 10 points, name this Norse god of mischief, who is bound beneath the earth until Ragnarok.

This is the name of Thor's weapon, a short-handled hammer made by the dwarves. A giant named Thrym once stole it and demanded the goddess Freya as his bride. For 10 points, name this hammer, which Thor uses to fight giants.

Warriors who died bravely in battle were carried by Valkyries to this hall, whose roof is made of golden shields. There they feast and fight each day in preparation for the final battle. Odin presides over it. For 10 points, name this hall of the slain in Asgard.

This is the realm of the Aesir gods, connected to the world of humans by a rainbow bridge. Its halls include Valhalla and the homes of Thor and Baldr. A great wall around it was built by a giant disguised as a builder. For 10 points, name this home of the Norse gods.

This enormous ash tree connects the nine worlds of Norse cosmology. A dragon gnaws at its roots, and a squirrel runs up and down its trunk carrying insults. The gods hold their daily council beneath it. For 10 points, name this world tree.

This is the final battle in which gods and giants destroy each other, after which the world sinks into the sea and is reborn. It is foretold to follow three winters without a summer. For 10 points, name this Norse doomsday, whose name means fate of the gods.

This giant wolf, a son of Loki, was raised among the gods, but they grew afraid of his growth and chained him on an island. A prophecy says that at Ragnarok he will break free, open his jaws from earth to sky, and swallow Odin. For 10 points, name this monstrous wolf.

This Vanir goddess rides in a chariot pulled by cats and owns a necklace called Brisingamen. She receives half of the warriors who die in battle. Her brother is Freyr. For 10 points, name this Norse goddess of love and beauty.

This goddess, the wife of Odin, knew the fates of all but never spoke of them. She asked every plant and animal to promise not to harm her son, but she overlooked the mistletoe. For 10 points, name this queen of the Norse gods and goddess of marriage.

This god was killed when his blind brother Hodr threw a mistletoe dart at him, guided by Loki. He was the brightest and most beloved of the gods. His death was one of the signs of the coming end of the world. For 10 points, name this son of Odin and Frigg.

This one-handed god of war and justice put his hand into the mouth of a wolf as a pledge of good faith. When the gods did not release the wolf, he lost the hand. For 10 points, name this Norse god who gave his name to Tuesday.

This watchman of the gods lives at the edge of heaven and can hear grass growing on the earth. He needs less sleep than a bird and will blow the Gjallarhorn to warn of the final battle. For 10 points, name this guardian of the rainbow bridge.

This is the name of the middle realm in Norse myth, home to humans. It is surrounded by an ocean in which a great serpent lies coiled. Its name means middle enclosure. For 10 points, name this world of men, between Asgard and the realm of giants.

This enormous sea serpent is a child of Loki and lies coiled around the world, biting its own tail. Thor once tried to catch it on a fishing trip, and they are fated to kill each other at Ragnarok. For 10 points, name this serpent, also called the Midgard Serpent.

This is the name of the eight-legged horse ridden by Odin. It was born when Loki, in the form of a mare, was impregnated by a stallion belonging to a giant builder. It is the fastest of all horses. For 10 points, name this steed.
This burning, three-colored bridge links Asgard to Midgard. It is guarded by Heimdall, and the sons of Muspell will break it at the end of the world. For 10 points, name this Norse rainbow bridge.

This goddess was the daughter of Loki who rules over a realm of the dishonored dead. She is described as half living and half corpse, with a face that is partly blue-black. Those who die of sickness or old age go to her. For 10 points, name this Norse goddess of the underworld.

Odin sends these two birds out each day to fly over the world and bring back news. Their names mean thought and memory. For 10 points, name this pair of ravens, who perch on the shoulders of the chief of the gods.

This Vanir god gave his magical sword to his servant Skirnir so that he could woo the giantess Gerd for him. He rides a golden boar named Gullinbursti, and he is the twin brother of Freya. For 10 points, name this Norse god of fertility, sunshine, and rain.

This goddess guards apples that keep the gods young. The giant Thiazi once kidnapped her, and the gods aged until Loki rescued her. For 10 points, name this Norse goddess of youth, the wife of the poet god Bragi.

The gods created the world from the body of this first giant, using his flesh for the earth, his blood for the seas, and his skull for the sky. He was slain by Odin and his brothers Vili and Ve. For 10 points, name this primeval frost giant.

These are the members of the main group of Norse gods, including Odin, Thor, and Baldr, who live in Asgard. They fought a war against the Vanir before the two groups made peace. For 10 points, name this group of Norse deities.

After Odin drank from his well, this being served as the keeper of wisdom beneath Yggdrasil. He was sent as a hostage to the Vanir, who beheaded him in anger, but Odin preserved the head with herbs and consulted it for counsel. For 10 points, name this wise figure.

This is the name of the yawning void that existed before creation in Norse myth. It lay between the realm of fire and the realm of ice, and where their forces met, the first giant came to be. For 10 points, name this primordial emptiness.

This weapon was made by dwarves, the sons of Ivaldi, during a contest arranged by Loki. It never misses its target, and oaths sworn on it cannot be broken. Odin hurled it over the ranks of the Vanir to begin the first war. For 10 points, name this spear of the chief Norse god.

This giantess's father was killed by the gods, so she traveled to Asgard in armor to demand compensation. She was allowed to choose a husband by seeing only his feet, and she picked a god of the sea thinking he was Baldr. For 10 points, name this winter goddess.

This sea god, the father of Freyr and Freya, was sent to live among the Aesir as a hostage. His marriage to the giantess Skadi failed because she could not bear the sea birds and he could not bear the mountains. For 10 points, name this Vanir god.

Loki cut off all of this goddess's golden hair as a prank. To avoid the anger of her husband, he swore to have dwarves forge a replacement of real gold that would grow like natural hair. For 10 points, name this wife of the thunder god.
Answer these questions about the nine worlds of Norse myth.
parts: Which realm, whose name means home of the giants, lies to the east of Midgard?
Which realm of ice and mist lies in the far north and is the home of the dead who did not die in battle?
Which realm of fire, home to the giant Surtr, lies in the far south?

q: Answer these questions about Norse gods and their groups.
parts: Which blind god accidentally killed his brother with a mistletoe dart?
Which group of Norse gods, which includes Njord, Freyr, and Freya, went to war with the Aesir?
Which god of poetry and eloquence is the husband of Idun?

q: Answer these questions about creatures of Norse myth.
parts: Which dragon gnaws at the roots of the world tree?
Which squirrel carries insults between the eagle at the top of the world tree and the dragon below?
Which primeval cow nourished the giant Ymir and licked the first god out of salty ice?

q: Answer these questions about treasures of the Norse gods.
parts: Which golden ring of Odin produces eight new rings every ninth night?
Which collapsible ship, owned by Freyr, can sail on any water and be folded into a pocket?
Which magical ribbon, made from the sound of a cat's footfall and the roots of a mountain, finally bound the wolf Fenrir?

q: Answer these questions about the Volsung saga.
parts: Which hero of the Volsung saga killed a dragon and bathed in its blood to become nearly invulnerable?
Which dwarf smith reforged the broken sword Gram and urged the hero to kill his own brother, a dragon?
Which valkyrie did the hero awaken from an enchanted sleep on a mountain ringed by fire?

q: Answer these questions about the end of the world.
parts: Which fire giant will burn the world with his flaming sword at Ragnarok?
Which silent son of Odin is fated to avenge his father by killing Fenrir?
Which blood-stained hound guards the gates of the underworld and will break free at Ragnarok?

q: Answer these questions about the adventures of Thor.
parts: What animals pull Thor's chariot across the sky?
Which giant with a heart of stone fought a duel against Thor, who defeated him with a hammer blow?
Which giant king tricked Thor with illusions, including a horn that was connected to the sea?

q: Answer these questions about the sources of Norse myth.
parts: Which seafaring Scandinavian people told and wrote down these stories?
Which Icelandic writer composed the Prose Edda in the thirteenth century?
Which poem of the Poetic Edda tells of the creation and destruction of the world as told by a seeress?

q: This god was shown with the head of a falcon topped by a solar disk. Each night he sailed his boat through the underworld, where he fought the serpent Apep, and each morning he was reborn. Pharaohs claimed to be his sons. For 10 points, name this Egyptian sun god.

This Egyptian god was murdered and dismembered by his brother Set. His wife gathered the pieces of his body and revived him long enough to conceive a son. He then became ruler of the dead and is often shown with green skin. For 10 points, name this Egyptian god of the afterlife.

This Egyptian goddess searched the Nile Delta for the pieces of her murdered husband. She used magic to protect her infant son Horus from Set. She is often shown with a throne on her head or with wings. For 10 points, name this goddess of magic and motherhood.
This Egyptian god was shown with the head of a jackal. He supervised the mummification of the dead and weighed the hearts of the deceased against a feather. For 10 points, name this god of embalming.

This Egyptian god was a falcon-headed sky god whose eye was a symbol of protection and healing. He lost an eye in a long battle to avenge the murder of his father. The pharaoh was seen as a living form of him. For 10 points, name this son of Isis and Osiris.

This Hindu god preserves the universe and returns to earth in ten avatars, including Rama and Krishna. He is shown with blue skin, reclining on the serpent Shesha. His mount is the eagle Garuda. For 10 points, name this member of the Hindu trimurti, the preserver.

This Hindu god wears a crescent moon and a cobra, and his third eye can destroy with fire. The river Ganges falls through his hair. He is called the destroyer in the trimurti and dances the cosmic dance of Nataraja. For 10 points, name this Hindu god.

This Hindu god has the head of an elephant, and he rides a mouse. He is the remover of obstacles, and a story says he broke off his own tusk to write the Mahabharata. For 10 points, name this son of Shiva and Parvati.

This Japanese goddess hid in a cave after being insulted by her brother, plunging the world into darkness. The other gods lured her out with a mirror and a raucous dance. The imperial family claimed descent from her. For 10 points, name this Shinto sun goddess.

This hero of Chinese myth was born from a stone egg and gained magical powers, including seventy-two transformations. He wields a staff that can change its size and rides a cloud. He accompanies the monk Tripitaka to India. For 10 points, name this Monkey King of Journey to the West.

This Egyptian god of writing and wisdom was shown with the head of an ibis. He was believed to have invented hieroglyphs, and he recorded the verdict when hearts were weighed in the underworld. His city was Hermopolis. For 10 points, name this scribe of the gods.

This Egyptian god of chaos and storms ruled the desert and was shown with the head of an unidentified animal with a curved snout. He murdered his brother Osiris and fought his nephew for the throne. For 10 points, name this god of disorder.

This feathered serpent god of the Toltecs and Aztecs was said to have created humans from the bones of earlier ages, which he sprinkled with his own blood. His rival was Tezcatlipoca. For 10 points, name this Mesoamerican god, whose name means feathered serpent.

This West African trickster takes the form of a spider. In Ashanti stories, he won all the tales in the world from the sky god by capturing a python, a leopard, and hornets. For 10 points, name this clever character who is a hero of many folktales.

This Sumerian king of Uruk was two-thirds god and one-third man. After the death of his friend, he journeyed to find the secret of immortality, only to lose a magical plant to a snake. For 10 points, name this hero of the world's oldest known epic.

This Mesopotamian goddess of love and war was known as Inanna to the Sumerians. She descended to the underworld, where she was stripped of her garments at each of seven gates. For 10 points, name this Babylonian goddess.

This monkey god, a devoted follower of Rama, leapt across the sea to find Sita. He set the city of Lanka on fire with his burning tail, and he carried an entire mountain of healing herbs. For 10 points, name this Hindu monkey deity.

This Hindu goddess is shown with black or dark blue skin, wearing a garland of skulls and with her tongue sticking out. She is a fierce form of the goddess Parvati and is often depicted dancing on Shiva. For 10 points, name this goddess of destruction and time.

This Hindu goddess of wealth and good fortune is shown sitting or standing on a lotus. She emerged from the churning of the ocean of milk and is worshipped during the festival of Diwali. For 10 points, name this wife of Vishnu.

This Hindu creator god has four faces and rides a swan. He sprang from a lotus growing from the navel of Vishnu. His wife is Saraswati. For 10 points, name this member of the Hindu trimurti, the creator.

This Polynesian demigod used a magical fishhook to pull up the Hawaiian islands from the sea. He also slowed the sun so that his mother's cloth could dry and stole fire from a bird. For 10 points, name this trickster hero of the Pacific.

This Hawaiian goddess lives in the crater of Halemaumau at Kilauea. She is said to be jealous and quick to anger, and visitors who take lava rocks from the islands are believed to suffer her curse. For 10 points, name this goddess of volcanoes.

This Irish hero of the Ulster Cycle was born as Setanta but took a new name after killing a guard dog. He wielded the spear Gae Bulg and held off the armies of Queen Medb alone. For 10 points, name this Hound of Ulster.

This trickster of many Native American traditions is both a creator and a fool. In some stories he steals fire or brings death into the world by bad judgment. For 10 points, name this canine character of the American Southwest and plains.

This Aztec god was born fully armed from his mother Coatlicue and killed his sister Coyolxauhqui. He demanded human sacrifices to keep the sun moving, and his shrine was at the top of the Great Temple of Tenochtitlan. For 10 points, name this war god whose name means blue hummingbird on the left.

This primordial saltwater goddess in Babylonian myth was a chaos monster who took the form of a dragon. A storm god split her body in two to form the heavens and the earth. For 10 points, name this mother of the first gods in the Enuma Elish, killed by Marduk.

This wild man was created by the gods from clay to be a rival to a king. He lived among animals until a woman named Shamhat civilized him, and he later helped slay Humbaba. For 10 points, name this friend of Gilgamesh.

This Chinese giant was born inside a cosmic egg. He separated earth from sky by growing taller for eighteen thousand years, and after his death his body became the mountains and rivers. For 10 points, name this first being of Chinese creation myth.

This Irish hero of the Fenian Cycle gained wisdom by tasting a salmon he was cooking. He led a band of warriors called the Fianna and is said to have built a causeway to Scotland to fight a rival giant. For 10 points, name this mythical hunter-warrior, also called Fionn mac Cumhaill.

This Japanese god was the male creator who, with his wife, formed the islands from a jeweled spear dipped in the sea. After fleeing the land of the dead, he washed in a river, and from his face were born Amaterasu, the moon god, and a storm god. For 10 points, name this Shinto creator god.
Answer these questions about Egyptian myth.
parts: Which goddess with the head of a cat protected homes and was worshipped at Bubastis?
Which goddess of truth and order wore an ostrich feather on her head?
Which sky goddess was shown arched over the earth, with her body covered in stars?

q: Answer these questions about Japanese myth.
parts: What is the name of the native religion of Japan, centered on worship of spirits called kami?
Which storm god, the brother of Amaterasu, killed an eight-headed serpent?
Which kami of rice and prosperity is associated with foxes as messengers?

q: Answer these questions about the Epic of Gilgamesh.
parts: Which city did Gilgamesh rule?
Which giant guardian of the Cedar Forest did Gilgamesh and his friend defeat?
Which man, the survivor of a great flood, told Gilgamesh the story of the gods' decision to destroy humanity?

q: Answer these questions about the Ramayana.
parts: Which ten-headed demon king of Lanka is the villain of the Ramayana?
Which wife of the hero Rama was abducted by the demon king?
Which monkey king allied with Rama to search for his kidnapped wife?

q: Answer these questions about Aztec myth.
parts: Which island city, on the site of modern Mexico City, was the capital of the Aztec Empire?
Which Aztec god of rain and fertility was worshipped atop the Great Temple alongside the war god?
Which Aztec god, whose name means smoking mirror, was the rival of Quetzalcoatl?

q: Answer these questions about Irish myth.
parts: Which tiny shoemaker of Irish folklore is said to guard a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow?
Which supernatural race of Irish gods, whose name means the people of the goddess Danu, were defeated by the Milesians?
Which Irish goddess of war and fate often appeared as a crow?

q: Answer these questions about Chinese myth.
parts: Which deity rules heaven in Chinese folk religion and is called the August Personage of Jade?
Which goddess repaired the broken sky with five colored stones after a great flood?
Which woman drank an elixir of immortality and flew to the moon, where she lives with a jade rabbit?

q: Answer these questions about the myths of Oceania.
parts: In Aboriginal Australian myth, which giant snake creates rivers and valleys while moving across the land?
In Aboriginal Australian belief, what is the name of the sacred time of creation and ancestral spirits?
Which Maori and Polynesian god of the sea is known as Kanaloa in Hawaii?

q: This philosopher claimed that his wisdom consisted only in knowing that he knew nothing. He compared himself to a gadfly stinging the sleepy city of Athens and said that the unexamined life is not worth living. He left no writings of his own. For 10 points, name this teacher of Plato.

This philosopher described a realm of perfect Forms of which the physical world is only a shadow. He wrote dialogues in which his teacher is the main speaker, including the Symposium and the Phaedo. His most famous student was Aristotle. For 10 points, name this Greek philosopher.

This philosopher analyzed four kinds of causes, including the material and the final cause, and he wrote on logic, ethics, politics, and biology. He tutored the young Alexander of Macedon. Raphael painted him gesturing toward the earth in The School of Athens. For 10 points, name this student of Plato.

This is the poison, made from a plant in the parsley family, that Athens gave to condemned prisoners. A famous philosopher drank a cup of it in 399 BC after being convicted of impiety, as told in the Phaedo. For 10 points, name this poison.

This work of Plato imagines a city ruled by philosopher-kings and argues that justice is harmony among the parts of the soul and city. It begins at the house of Cephalus and features a debate with Thrasymachus. For 10 points, name this dialogue about justice, an enormous work of political philosophy.

In this allegory, prisoners are chained in an underground chamber and see only shadows cast on a wall by a fire. One prisoner escapes, is dazzled by the sun, and returns to tell others what he saw. For 10 points, name this allegory from Plato's Republic that illustrates his theory of knowledge.

This Milesian is often called the first philosopher in the Western tradition. He argued that everything is made of water and is said to have predicted a solar eclipse. For 10 points, name this Greek thinker, the first of the Seven Sages.

This Greek philosopher and mathematician founded a religious brotherhood in southern Italy that believed in reincarnation. He is famous for a theorem about right triangles and said that all things are numbers. For 10 points, name this Greek thinker.

This Greek philosopher is said to have lived in a large ceramic jar and walked around in daylight with a lamp searching for an honest man. When Alexander the Great offered him a favor, he asked the king to step out of his sunlight. For 10 points, name this Cynic.

This Roman emperor wrote a private journal of reflections while on military campaign in central Europe. Written in Greek, those Meditations advise accepting what cannot be controlled. He is the last of the Five Good Emperors. For 10 points, name this Stoic emperor.

This philosopher argued that the world is in constant flux, saying that you cannot step into the same river twice. He believed that fire is the fundamental substance and that the logos governs all change. For 10 points, name this Ephesian known as the Obscure.

This philosopher developed atomism, arguing that all matter consists of tiny indivisible particles moving in a void. His teacher was Leucippus, and he was nicknamed the Laughing Philosopher. For 10 points, name this thinker from Abdera.

This philosopher taught that pleasure is the highest good, but defined it mainly as freedom from pain and disturbance. He gathered followers in a garden in Athens and argued that death is nothing to us. For 10 points, name this founder of a school of philosophy.

This former slave and lame philosopher taught that we should focus only on what is up to us. His lectures were recorded by his student Arrian as the Discourses and the Enchiridion. For 10 points, name this Stoic of Hierapolis.

This Roman philosopher served as tutor to the emperor Nero and wrote Letters to Lucilius and On the Shortness of Life. He was ordered to take his own life in 65 AD. For 10 points, name this Stoic and playwright.

This school was founded by Plato in a grove outside Athens and lasted for centuries. Aristotle studied there for about twenty years. For 10 points, name this first institution of higher learning in the Western world.
This school in Athens was founded by Aristotle in a grove sacred to Apollo. Its members were nicknamed peripatetics because they discussed ideas while walking. For 10 points, name this school.

This work by Aristotle examines the best life for human beings and argues that virtue is a mean between excess and deficiency. It is named for his father or his son. For 10 points, name this treatise on ethics.

This school of thought took its name from a painted porch in Athens. It taught that virtue is the only good and that one should accept fate calmly. For 10 points, name this school followed by Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius.

This Greek school took its name from the word for dog. Its followers rejected wealth, fame, and social conventions in favor of living according to nature. Antisthenes is considered its founder. For 10 points, name this philosophy, associated with Diogenes.

This method of teaching involves asking a series of probing questions in order to expose contradictions in a person's beliefs. It is named for an Athenian philosopher and is often used in law schools. For 10 points, name this question-and-answer method.

This type of reasoning, studied by Aristotle, draws a conclusion from two premises, such as all men are mortal, Socrates is a man, so Socrates is mortal. For 10 points, name this form of deductive argument.

This Greek word, usually translated as flourishing or happiness, is for Aristotle the highest aim of human life. It comes from words meaning good and spirit. For 10 points, name this concept central to Greek ethics.

These were itinerant teachers in classical Greece who charged fees to teach rhetoric and the art of persuasion. Plato criticized them for treating truth as relative. Gorgias and Protagoras belonged to this group. For 10 points, name these paid teachers.

This philosopher from Elea wrote a poem in which a goddess describes the way of truth and the way of opinion. He argued that what exists is one, unchanging, and eternal, and that change is an illusion. For 10 points, name this Eleatic thinker, whose student Zeno defended his ideas.
This student of Parmenides argued that motion is impossible through paradoxes. In one, a swift runner can never overtake a slow tortoise. For 10 points, name this Eleatic philosopher.

This Milesian philosopher proposed that the origin of all things is an infinite, indefinite substance. He is credited with creating an early map of the known world. For 10 points, name this student of Thales, who named that substance the apeiron.

This philosopher, said to have accompanied Alexander the Great to India, founded a school that taught suspension of judgment as the path to peace of mind. For 10 points, name this founder of Skepticism, called Pyrrhonism after him.

This Sophist from Abdera was a friend of the statesman Pericles. He claimed that man is the measure of all things, a statement taken to mean that truth is relative to the individual. For 10 points, name this Greek thinker, the namesake of a Platonic dialogue.

This philosopher, born in Roman Egypt, taught in Rome and believed that all things emanate from a single ineffable source called the One. His student Porphyry edited his writings into the Enneads. For 10 points, name this founder of Neoplatonism.
Answer these questions about the dialogues of Plato.
parts: Which dialogue is set at a drinking party where guests give speeches in praise of love?
Which dialogue shows Socrates in prison, refusing to escape despite his friend's urging?
Which dialogue offers an account of the creation of the cosmos and mentions the lost island of Atlantis?

q: Answer these questions about the works of Aristotle.
parts: Which work discusses tragedy, plot, and catharsis?
Which work, whose title means after the physics, discusses being and first causes?
Which collection of six texts, including the Categories and Prior Analytics, makes up his writings on logic?

q: Answer these questions about Roman philosophers.
parts: Which Roman orator and statesman wrote On Duties and was killed on the orders of Mark Antony?
Which Epicurean poet wrote the epic On the Nature of Things?
Which Roman writer, imprisoned under the Gothic king Theodoric, composed The Consolation of Philosophy?

q: Answer these questions about the trial of Socrates.
parts: In which city was Socrates tried and executed?
Which oracle at Apollo's sanctuary declared that no one was wiser than Socrates?
Which soldier and historian wrote a Memorabilia and an Apology defending the memory of Socrates?

q: Answer these questions about the life of Aristotle.
parts: Which Macedonian conqueror did Aristotle tutor?
In which northern Greek town was Aristotle born?
Which student succeeded Aristotle as head of his school and wrote on botany and character types?

q: Answer these questions about opponents of Socrates in Plato's dialogues.
parts: Which Sophist from Leontini gives his name to a dialogue about rhetoric?
Which Sophist argues in the first book of the Republic that justice is the interest of the stronger?
Which character in that same dialogue on rhetoric argues that might makes right?

q: Answer these questions about key Greek words.
parts: Which English word comes from a Greek phrase meaning love of wisdom?
Which Greek word, meaning word or reason, was used by Heraclitus and the Stoics for the rational principle of the universe?
Which Greek word for virtue or excellence is central to Socratic ethics?

q: Answer these questions about the founders and leaders of Stoicism.
parts: Which philosopher from Cyprus founded the Stoic school in Athens?
Which third head of the Stoic school wrote hundreds of treatises on logic?
Which second head of the Stoic school wrote the Hymn to Zeus?

q: This philosopher imagined an evil demon who deceives him about everything and concluded that his own existence cannot be doubted because he is thinking. He argued that mind and body are separate substances. His Discourse on Method begins with systematic doubt. For 10 points, name this French author of Meditations on First Philosophy, who said "I think, therefore I am."

This English philosopher argued that people have natural rights to life, liberty, and property and that governments exist only by the consent of the governed. His Two Treatises of Government influenced Thomas Jefferson. For 10 points, name this author of An Essay Concerning Human Understanding.

This philosopher from Konigsberg argued that we can know only the world as it appears to us and never things as they are in themselves. His major works include the Critique of Pure Reason and the Critique of Practical Reason. For 10 points, name this German Enlightenment thinker.

This German philosopher declared that God is dead and called for the coming of the Übermensch. He also wrote Thus Spoke Zarathustra and Beyond Good and Evil. His idea of the will to power opposed traditional Christian morality. For 10 points, name this philosopher.

This German philosopher and economist argued that history is driven by class struggle and that capitalism would be replaced by communism. He wrote Das Kapital while living in London. For 10 points, name this author, with Friedrich Engels, of The Communist Manifesto.

This Swiss-born philosopher argued that humans are naturally good but are corrupted by society. He began a famous book with the line that man is born free, but everywhere he is in chains. He also wrote Emile. For 10 points, name this French Enlightenment thinker, author of The Social Contract.

This French Enlightenment writer championed religious tolerance and freedom of speech, and he wrote the satire Candide. He was exiled to England and spent his last years at Ferney. For 10 points, name this author, whose real name was Francois-Marie Arouet.

This English philosopher and statesman wrote the Novum Organum, which advocated gathering evidence through experiment and induction. He is credited with the saying that knowledge is power, and he served as Lord Chancellor. For 10 points, name this father of the scientific method and author of New Atlantis.

This French philosopher wrote Being and Nothingness and the play No Exit, which includes the line that hell is other people. He argued that existence precedes essence. He refused the Nobel Prize in Literature. For 10 points, name this French existentialist.

This moral theory holds that an action is right if it produces the greatest good for the greatest number of people. It was developed by Jeremy Bentham and refined by John Stuart Mill. For 10 points, name this consequentialist philosophy.

This English philosopher wrote that without a strong government, life in the state of nature would be solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short. He lived through the English Civil War and defended absolute monarchy. For 10 points, name this author of Leviathan.

This Scottish philosopher argued that we have no rational basis for believing in cause and effect, only habit. His Treatise of Human Nature claimed that the self is a bundle of perceptions. He awoke Kant from his dogmatic slumber. For 10 points, name this skeptical empiricist.

This English philosopher wrote On Liberty, which argued that society may limit individual freedom only to prevent harm to others. He also wrote The Subjection of Women, in collaboration with Harriet Taylor. For 10 points, name this utilitarian who wrote Utilitarianism.

This English philosopher designed a circular prison called the Panopticon and requested that his preserved body be displayed after death. He wrote An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation, which measured actions by pleasure and pain. For 10 points, name this founder of modern utilitarianism.

This Danish philosopher wrote Fear and Trembling, which discusses Abraham's near-sacrifice of Isaac, and introduced the idea of the leap of faith. He published many works under pseudonyms and broke off his engagement to Regine Olsen. For 10 points, name this father of existentialism.

This German philosopher wrote the Phenomenology of Spirit and argued that history advances through a dialectical process toward freedom. He taught at the University of Berlin, and his ideas strongly influenced Marx. For 10 points, name this absolute idealist.

This French philosopher wrote The Second Sex, which says that one is not born but rather becomes a woman. She was a lifelong partner of Jean-Paul Sartre. For 10 points, name this founder of modern feminist philosophy.

This Algerian-born French writer argued in The Myth of Sisyphus that life is absurd and that one must imagine Sisyphus happy. He also wrote the novels The Stranger and The Plague. For 10 points, name this winner of the 1957 Nobel Prize in Literature.

This English philosopher wrote A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, arguing that women should receive an education equal to men. She was the mother of the author of Frankenstein. For 10 points, name this early feminist thinker.

This movement, associated with Kierkegaard, Sartre, and Camus, emphasizes individual freedom, choice, and responsibility in a world without given meaning. For 10 points, name this philosophical movement.

This principle states that one should act only according to a maxim that one could will to become a universal law. It was proposed in the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals by a German philosopher. For 10 points, name this ethical principle.

This Latin phrase, meaning blank slate, describes the idea that the mind at birth has no innate ideas and is filled by experience. An English empiricist popularized it. For 10 points, name this phrase.

This 1651 work begins with a frontispiece showing a giant crowned figure made up of many tiny people. It argues that people give up some freedom to a sovereign in exchange for protection from violence. For 10 points, name this work named for a biblical sea monster.

This theory in philosophy holds that all knowledge comes from sensory experience rather than from innate ideas. It is usually contrasted with rationalism and is associated with British thinkers. For 10 points, name this theory of knowledge.

This Irish bishop argued that material objects exist only as perceptions in minds, summing up his position as to be is to be perceived. His Treatise concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge defended this immaterialism. For 10 points, name this philosopher, the namesake of a California city.

This Dutch philosopher was excommunicated from his Jewish community in Amsterdam and earned a living grinding lenses. His Ethics is written in the form of geometric proofs and identifies God with nature. For 10 points, name this rationalist.

This German rationalist argued that the universe is made up of simple, windowless units called monads. He claimed that we live in the best of all possible worlds and is credited with independently inventing calculus. For 10 points, name this philosopher.

This French baron wrote Persian Letters and The Spirit of the Laws, in which he argued that governmental power should be divided among separate branches. His ideas deeply influenced the framers of the United States Constitution. For 10 points, name this political philosopher.

This German pessimist argued that the world is driven by a blind, striving force he called the will. His main work, The World as Will and Representation, influenced Nietzsche and Wagner. For 10 points, name this philosopher.

This French mathematician and philosopher argued that it is rational to bet on the existence of God. He wrote the Pensees and the Provincial Letters and invented an early mechanical calculator. For 10 points, name this man who has a law of fluid pressure and a triangle named after him.

q: According to the Gospels of Matthew and Luke, Jesus was born in this town near Jerusalem, where shepherds came to see the baby. Wise men from the East are said to have followed a star to this place. Joseph and Mary traveled here for a census. For 10 points, name this town in the West Bank known as the birthplace of Jesus.

On this holiday, many Christians exchange gifts and attend church services featuring carols and nativity scenes. Decorated evergreen trees and Advent wreaths are common symbols of its season. Churches often hold a candlelit midnight service on its eve. For 10 points, name this holiday celebrated on December 25 that marks the birth of Jesus.

This Sunday begins Holy Week and recalls the day Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a donkey while crowds laid down branches and cloaks. Churches often hand out woven fronds on this day. It falls one week before Easter. For 10 points, name this Sunday named for the branches waved by the crowd.

This holiday, held fifty days after Easter, commemorates the descent of the Holy Spirit on the apostles. The Book of Acts says they were gathered together when tongues of fire appeared above them and they began to speak in other languages. Some call it the birthday of the Church. For 10 points, name this feast whose name comes from the Greek for fiftieth.

Many Christians give up a favorite food or habit during this forty-day period of fasting and prayer before Easter. It echoes the forty days Jesus spent in the wilderness. It begins on Ash Wednesday and ends before Holy Week. For 10 points, name this season of repentance and preparation before Easter.

On this day, Christians receive a cross of ashes on the forehead as a sign of repentance. Priests often say the words remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return. It is the first day of a forty-day season of preparation. For 10 points, name this Wednesday that begins Lent.

This man was a Pharisee who persecuted early Christians until a vision of Jesus blinded him on the road to Damascus. He then made missionary journeys around the Mediterranean. Thirteen letters in the New Testament are traditionally attributed to him. For 10 points, name this apostle to the Gentiles, formerly called Saul.

This disciple is said to have betrayed Jesus to the authorities for thirty pieces of silver. He identified Jesus by greeting him with a kiss in the Garden of Gethsemane. Later he is said to have died by hanging himself. For 10 points, name this apostle whose last name probably refers to a place or group, and whose name has become a synonym for traitor.

Leonardo da Vinci painted a famous mural of this event in the refectory of a Milan monastery. Jesus is shown seated at a long table with his twelve disciples, just after saying that one of them would betray him. During this meal Jesus shared bread and wine, which is the origin of a Christian ritual. For 10 points, name this final meal before the Crucifixion.

Jesus was baptized by John in this river, and the Gospels say the Holy Spirit descended like a dove. Today, many churches use water to perform a ritual in which a person is welcomed into the faith, either by sprinkling or by immersion. For 10 points, name this Christian sacrament of initiation that uses water.

In this Christian rite, believers eat consecrated bread and drink wine or grape juice to remember the sacrifice of Jesus. Catholics believe the elements become the body and blood of Christ, a doctrine called transubstantiation. It is also known as the Eucharist or the Lord's Supper. For 10 points, name this sacrament, a word that also means sharing in something together.

Christians who profess this doctrine believe that God exists as three persons in one being. The Nicene Creed lays it out, and the shamrock is sometimes used as a teaching symbol for it. Its three persons are the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For 10 points, name this central Christian doctrine of the three-in-one God.

This is the last book of the Christian Bible. Its author, named John, writes of visions that include four horsemen, seven seals, a great beast, and a new heaven and new earth. It is full of symbolic imagery and is sometimes called the Apocalypse. For 10 points, name this final book of the New Testament.

Many of these 150 poems are traditionally credited to King David. One of them begins The Lord is my shepherd, and they are used as hymns and prayers in both Jewish and Christian worship. For 10 points, name this book of the Old Testament that is a collection of sacred songs and poems.

In a parable told by Jesus, a traveler is beaten by robbers and left by the road. A priest and a Levite pass him by, but a man from a region despised by the traveler's people stops to bandage his wounds and pay for his care. For 10 points, name this parable whose title now describes a person who helps strangers in need.

In a parable from the Gospel of Luke, a younger son demands his inheritance, leaves home, and wastes it all on reckless living. When famine strikes, he returns home, expecting to be punished. Instead, his father throws a feast and the older brother complains. For 10 points, name this parable about forgiveness and a returning child.

Christians recite this prayer, which Jesus taught his disciples, beginning with the words Our Father, who art in heaven. It includes the lines give us this day our daily bread and forgive us our trespasses. For 10 points, name this most widely used Christian prayer.

In this speech, delivered from a hillside in Galilee, Jesus says blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. It begins with the Beatitudes and includes teachings such as turning the other cheek and loving your enemies. For 10 points, name this famous discourse found in the Gospel of Matthew.

Legend says this man used a three-leaf plant to explain the Trinity and drove snakes out of Ireland. Born in Roman Britain, he was captured by raiders as a teenager and later returned to Ireland as a missionary. For 10 points, name this patron saint of Ireland, whose feast day is March 17.

This Italian man gave up the wealth of his merchant father to live in poverty. He is said to have preached to birds and tamed a wolf in the town of Gubbio. He founded an order of friars, and many people ask for his blessing on animals. For 10 points, name this saint from Assisi.

This French teenager said she heard the voices of saints telling her to help the crown prince reach the throne. She led an army to lift the siege of Orleans during the Hundred Years War. She was captured, tried for heresy, and burned at the stake in 1431. For 10 points, name this saint, known as the Maid of Orleans.

This Catholic nun, born in what is now North Macedonia, founded the Missionaries of Charity in Calcutta, India. She spent decades caring for the poor, sick, and dying, and she won the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize. She was canonized as a saint in 2016. For 10 points, name this nun known for her service to the poor.

This 16th-century movement began when Martin Luther posted his Ninety-five Theses. It split Western Christianity and led to the founding of Lutheran, Reformed, and Anglican churches. John Calvin and Huldrych Zwingli were also leaders. For 10 points, name this religious upheaval that created Protestantism.

This independent city-state located inside Rome is the smallest country in the world by area. It is home to Saint Peter's Basilica, the Sistine Chapel, and the Pope. For 10 points, name this tiny nation that is the center of the Roman Catholic Church.

Pope Urban II launched the first of these medieval military campaigns in 1095 with a speech at Clermont. Christian armies from Europe sought to capture Jerusalem and other holy sites from Muslim rulers. Richard the Lionheart and Saladin met during the Third of these campaigns. For 10 points, name these religious wars of the Middle Ages.

This season of the Christian calendar begins about four weeks before Christmas. Families often light candles on a wreath, one each Sunday, and open small doors on a calendar that counts down the days. The word comes from the Latin for coming. For 10 points, name this season of waiting before Christmas.

On January 6, many Christians celebrate this feast, which commemorates the visit of the Magi to the infant Jesus. Some churches observe it as the end of the twelve days of Christmas. Its name comes from a Greek word meaning manifestation. For 10 points, name this feast, also called Three Kings Day.

The Gospel of Luke says this archangel appeared to Mary to announce that she would bear a son named Jesus. In the Book of Daniel this angel also explains visions to the prophet. In Islam, the same being brought revelations to Muhammad. For 10 points, name this messenger angel often shown holding a trumpet.

This prophet baptized people in the Jordan River and preached repentance. He wore clothes of camel hair, and his diet was locusts and wild honey. He baptized Jesus and was later beheaded at the request of Salome. For 10 points, name this cousin of Jesus.

This day of the Christian calendar remembers the crucifixion of Jesus. Churches often hold solemn services, and many Christians fast or follow the Stations of the Cross. It falls two days before Easter Sunday. For 10 points, name this Friday of Holy Week.

q: This word names the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, which are traditionally credited to Moses. A handwritten scroll of these books is kept in the ark of a synagogue and read aloud in weekly portions. The readers use a pointer called a yad. For 10 points, name this sacred text, whose name means teaching or law.

This prophet was found as a baby in a basket among the reeds of the Nile. He confronted the pharaoh with ten plagues, led the Israelites out of Egypt, and received the law on Mount Sinai. For 10 points, name this Hebrew leader who is credited as the author of the Torah.
